tagline: A form persists by becoming historically different.
definition: The quality of extending through, developing across, or being studied over time, especially when changes between successive states matter more than the relations within a single temporal snapshot alone.
etymology: From diachronic, built from Greek dia, through, and chronos, time; the abstract suffix marks the quality of temporal development or comparison.

sections.heading: MEANING IN MOTION
sections.text: A diachronic account of English follows changes in pronunciation, grammar, or vocabulary across periods; a synchronic account studies how those elements relate at a selected time. Tracking how one neighborhood changes from workshops to apartments offers a comparable historical example.

sections.heading: THE CRUCIAL DISTINCTION
sections.text: Diachronicity is not simply the presence of dates: it directs attention toward development, persistence, rupture, and sequence. Nor does it imply inevitable progress. The distinction concerns analytical perspective, and a strong explanation can combine synchronic descriptions of different moments with a diachronic account of their transformations.

sections.heading: SEQUENCE IS NOT DESTINY
sections.text: A series of historical states can display transformation without proving improvement or a necessary destination. Later does not automatically mean better, and a present institution need not be the purpose of its predecessors. Diachronic analysis becomes stronger when it explains contingencies as well as continuities.

sections.heading: CHOOSING WHAT PERSISTS
sections.text: To compare successive states, an analyst must decide what counts as the same language, neighborhood, or practice across change. Those decisions are substantive. The shared foundation in the artwork offers one continuity, while altered buildings ask which social relations survive, disappear, or acquire new names.

literary: Under the avenue's newest name the cobbles kept an older traffic, while vowels, rents, and chimney smoke changed tenants, each century mispronouncing the city it confidently believed complete.
art_caption: Four architectural states share a ground line while their materials, heights, and uses change.
